summary: Tankers burn in the Strait of Hormuz as Trump threatens Iran again, Nvidia loses the founder who built it, and Netanyahu's rival gets the first shot at governing Israel.

stories.headline: Two supertankers burn in Hormuz as Trump says he could strike Iran again
stories.dek: Iran says the ships ignored its warnings. Washington says it no longer needs a deal with Tehran.
what: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels of oil between them were disabled by explosions late on Wednesday. They were using a southern route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran calls unauthorised. Iran's regular army separately said tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines east of the strait. The ships and their flags have not been named, and there is no independent confirmation yet.

On Thursday, President Trump wrote that the US no longer needs a deal with Iran. He then told an interviewer he would order new strikes without hesitation if things moved the wrong way, possibly right away. Israeli media report that US Central Command has told Israel's military to prepare for possible renewed action.
background: The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. A ceasefire followed in April and the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but talks stalled and clashes resumed.

Since then the fight has centred on the strait. Iran uses its control of the waterway as leverage. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and is helping tankers get through on routes Iran says are off-limits.
stories.why: About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through Hormuz. Every attack there pushes up oil and shipping costs, which feed into fuel and food prices around the world, Europe included.
stories.say: The Iran war never really ended. It moved to the Strait of Hormuz, and now both sides are threatening to escalate again.

terms.def: The narrow channel between Iran and Oman that links the Gulf to the open ocean. It is the world's most important oil chokepoint.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard, an elite military force separate from the regular army that answers to the Supreme Leader.
Using warships to stop ships from entering or leaving a country's ports.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's CEO after 33 years
stories.dek: Finance chief Colette Kress takes over for now, after a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy.
what: Nvidia said in a regulatory filing that Jensen Huang has resigned. He co-founded the company in 1993 and has run it ever since. Chief financial officer Colette Kress becomes interim CEO and keeps her finance job. The board named Harvey Jones its first-ever chair while it searches for a permanent successor.

Huang's exit follows a board investigation into his affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing. Investigators are also reported to be looking at whether a company linked to her helped smuggle restricted US chips into China. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.
background: Nvidia makes the chips that power most of the world's AI systems, and that has made it a company worth more than $4 trillion. Huang kept decision-making concentrated in his own hands and never named a successor, so analysts have long described him as the company's single biggest risk.
The US restricts sales of its most advanced AI chips to China, which is why any link to Beijing is so sensitive.
stories.why: Nvidia sits at the centre of both the AI boom and the US–China tech rivalry. Who runs it, and whether its chips are leaking to China, matters for markets, for AI and for national security.
stories.say: Nvidia just lost the founder who turned it into the engine of the AI boom, and the reason is a national-security scandal, not the business.

terms.def: A temporary boss who runs a company until a permanent one is chosen.
Government rules that limit which technology can be sold abroad. The US bars sales of its most advanced AI chips to China.

stories.headline: Netanyahu's rival Eisenkot gets the first shot at forming Israel's government
stories.dek: The former army chief has 28 days to build a majority after an election that left neither camp able to govern alone.
what: President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party, the mandate to form a government on 8 November, passing over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. 67 of the Knesset's 120 members recommended Eisenkot. That count includes Arab-led parties that some of his likely partners refuse to rely on, so his own bloc lacks a clear majority.
He has 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension. If he fails, the mandate goes to Netanyahu, who would get 28 days with no extension.
background: Israel voted on 27 October. No party has ever won a majority alone, so every government is a coalition. After an election the president consults all the parties and gives the mandate to whoever looks most likely to put together 61 of the 120 seats.
Netanyahu is Israel's longest-serving prime minister and has led a religious-nationalist coalition. Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the army.
stories.why: This could end the Netanyahu era. The next government will set Israel's course on Gaza, Iran and its relationship with the US.
stories.say: Netanyahu is on the outside for now. Eisenkot has the mandate, but he still has to turn 67 recommendations into 61 reliable votes.

terms.def: Israel's parliament, which has 120 seats.
The president's formal request to a party leader to try to form a government.

stories.headline: G7 warns China over its pressure east of Taiwan
stories.dek: The big democracies say Beijing's patrols threaten shipping. Taipei fears they are rehearsals for a blockade.
what: After meeting in Paris this week, foreign ministers of the G7 (the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada) said China's increasingly assertive activity in the waters east of Taiwan threatens regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of shipping.
It is the group's strongest joint statement on the issue so far. Until now only some members had raised it. Beijing rejected the criticism as interference in its internal affairs.
background: China claims Taiwan as its territory and has never ruled out using force to take it. Taiwan's government rejects that claim.

Since June, China's coast guard has been patrolling regularly off Taiwan's east coast. That is the side facing the Pacific, which Taipei counts on for supplies from allies in a crisis. Taiwanese officials believe China is practising a maritime blockade that would use military, coast-guard and civilian ships together.
stories.why: Taiwan makes most of the world's most advanced chips. A blockade could cut it off without a shot being fired, and the damage would reach phones, cars and AI everywhere.
stories.say: The worry over Taiwan has shifted from invasion to blockade, and China's patrols on the east coast look like practice for one.

terms.def: A club of seven large democratic economies (the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada) that coordinate policy. The EU also takes part.
The principle that ships of every country may sail through international waters without interference.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine hold their first US-brokered talks in nine months
stories.dek: Two days of meetings in Abu Dhabi covered ending the war and post-war security, while the strikes went on.
what: Delegations from Kyiv and Moscow met in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November, with Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner mediating. The agenda covered ending the war, security arrangements for afterwards, de-escalation and humanitarian steps.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks very productive but said a lot of work remained. Russia objects to European involvement, although it says the EU could join at a later stage.
background: Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022. The last US-mediated round took place in February this year, before the US–Israeli war with Iran pulled Washington's attention away.
The front lines are largely deadlocked, and both sides keep up long-range strikes. Russia fired 162 drones and a ballistic missile at Ukraine the night before the talks opened.
stories.why: This is the first real diplomatic movement in months. Any deal would redraw Europe's security map, but both sides are still holding to their core demands, especially on territory.
stories.say: Russia and Ukraine are talking again for the first time since February, but neither side has moved on the big question of territory.

terms.def: Promises from other countries to defend Ukraine, or help it, if Russia attacks again after a deal.
Negotiations between three parties. Here: Russia, Ukraine and the US as mediator.

stories.headline: After winning the Senate, Democrats fight over who should lead it
stories.dek: Chris Van Hollen is moving toward a challenge to Chuck Schumer, the party's Senate leader for nearly a decade.
what: Democrats' sweeping wins in the 3 November midterms give them control of the Senate from January, which would make Chuck Schumer majority leader again. But several senators and senators-elect won't commit to backing him.

Maryland's Chris Van Hollen, a favourite of progressives, first said he was focused on a possible 2028 presidential run, then reopened the door. NPR reported on Friday that he now says he will challenge Schumer. Michigan's Elissa Slotkin has also said she is weighing a run.
background: Each party's senators choose their leader by a simple majority in a closed vote, usually held a few weeks after an election. This one is expected next month.
The majority leader decides which bills reach the Senate floor and when, which makes it one of the most powerful jobs in Washington.
stories.why: Whoever wins will steer how Democrats use their new majority against President Trump: investigations, the Iran war and cost-of-living bills.
stories.say: Democrats won the Senate and immediately started fighting over whether Schumer is still the right person to run it.

terms.def: US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, covering all House seats and about a third of the Senate.
All of a party's members in a chamber, acting as a group.

stories.headline: US prices rise faster than expected, and the Fed may raise rates again
stories.dek: Consumer prices climbed 0.4% in October, in the last big inflation reading before the Fed's December meeting.
what: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, more than the 0.3% economists expected. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3% for the third month running, against forecasts of 0.2%. Food, services and shelter did most of the pushing.
Unusually, there is no year-on-year figure. Last year's government shutdown meant October 2025 prices were never collected. The last annual reading, for September, was 3.7%.
background: The Federal Reserve aims for 2% inflation. With prices running well above that, markets now expect it to raise interest rates at its 8–9 December meeting rather than cut them.
Higher rates make borrowing more expensive for everyone from home buyers to companies, which is how the Fed tries to cool spending and slow price rises.
stories.why: US interest rates move the dollar and markets worldwide. When the Fed raises rates, borrowing gets dearer and stock markets often wobble, well beyond the US.
stories.say: US inflation is still running well above target, so the Fed is now expected to raise rates in December, not cut them.

terms.def: The Consumer Price Index, which tracks the price of a typical basket of goods and services. It is the main measure of inflation.
Inflation without food and energy, whose prices swing a lot. It shows the underlying trend better.
When a central bank raises its main interest rate to slow inflation.

stories.headline: COP31 climate summit hits halfway in Antalya, without the US
stories.dek: Leaders spoke this week. The hard bargaining over money and fossil fuels runs until 20 November.
what: World leaders addressed the UN climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, on 11 and 12 November. About 190 countries are taking part in the two-week talks, which end on 20 November.

Turkey holds the presidency while Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, runs the negotiations. It is the first time the role has been split between two countries. The hosts want countries to sign up to a goal of electrifying more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from about a fifth today, and to an 'Antalya Pledge' on AI's energy use.
background: A COP is the yearly meeting of the countries that signed the UN climate treaty. The 2015 Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2°C, and ideally to 1.5°C.

President Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and sent no officials, although a group from Congress is attending. Money is the main fight: poorer countries want more climate finance, and the EU has warned there is little appetite for new pledges.
stories.why: The world is not on track for the 1.5°C goal. What gets agreed here shapes energy policy, and with it energy prices and jobs, for years.
stories.say: COP31 is happening without the US at the table, so the real test is whether Europe, China and the big emerging economies keep pushing on their own.

terms.def: Conference of the Parties: the annual UN climate summit. COP31 is the 31st.
Money from richer countries to help poorer ones cut emissions and adapt to climate damage.

stories.headline: America's astronaut taxi is heading for retirement
stories.dek: SpaceX plans to phase out Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 around 2030 to focus on Starship, leaving NASA leaning on Boeing.
what: NASA chief Jared Isaacman has confirmed that SpaceX intends to wind down Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon as it puts its effort into Starship, its giant next-generation rocket. SpaceX will keep flying to the International Space Station until the station retires around 2030. It has told NASA it has no current plans to fly people to low Earth orbit on Starship.

That leaves Boeing's Starliner as NASA's backup. Its only crewed flight, in 2024, ended with its two astronauts coming home on a SpaceX capsule. NASA is paying Boeing $359 million to get it back on track, with an uncrewed test flight around the turn of the year and a crewed one in 2028.
background: Since 2020, Crew Dragon has been the workhorse that carries NASA's astronauts to the space station. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell argues the company has to make its own products obsolete before a competitor does.
stories.why: It shows how much of the West's access to space now depends on the business decisions of a single company.
stories.say: SpaceX is retiring the capsule that made it NASA's taxi so it can bet everything on Starship, and NASA's plan B is Boeing.

terms.def: The zone up to about 2,000 km above Earth, where the space station and most satellites fly.
SpaceX's fully reusable super-heavy rocket, the largest ever built.

briefs.text: President Trump warned Mexico over a migrant caravan heading north. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum says her authorities are working to send the migrants home.
Brazil's Lula, fresh from re-election, is among the leaders addressing COP31. Climate activists hailed his win.
Today, 13 November, is World Kindness Day.

quiz.q: Who is running Nvidia now that Jensen Huang has resigned?
quiz.explain: Kress, Nvidia's CFO since 2013, is interim CEO. Harvey Jones became the board's first chair.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz?
quiz.explain: About one-fifth, which is why trouble there moves oil prices worldwide.

quiz.q: How long does Gadi Eisenkot have to form a government, before any extension?
quiz.explain: 28 days, which the president can extend by 14. If he fails, Netanyahu gets 28 days with no extension.

quiz.q: Why is there no year-on-year US inflation figure for October?
options: October 2025 prices were never collected because of a shutdown
It was delayed by the midterms
quiz.explain: The 2025 government shutdown left no October 2025 data to compare against.

quiz.q: Which country is running the negotiations at COP31, while Turkey hosts?
quiz.explain: Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen leads the talks. It's the first time the role has been split between two countries.
